title: 390 Gravitational Waves In, and Black Hole Astronomy Is Just Getting Started
hook: The latest gravitational-wave catalog leaps to 390 confirmed detections — including the clearest signal ever caught and evidence some black holes are built from earlier mergers.
key_points: The newest gravitational-wave catalog adds 161 new black hole mergers, bringing the total to 390 detections.
It includes the clearest gravitational-wave signal recorded to date and the most precisely located merger yet.
Growing evidence suggests some detected black holes formed from earlier black hole mergers, not just collapsed stars.
Detections now arrive several times a week, marking a new phase for gravitational-wave astronomy.
content_html: In 2015, LIGO's first gravitational-wave detection was a single, hard-won signal. A decade later, the field has become a firehose: the latest catalog release adds 161 newly confirmed black hole mergers in one go, pushing the running total to 390.
extra_html: As ScienceDaily reports, the new catalog features some standout events — the clearest gravitational-wave signal ever recorded and the most precisely pinpointed black hole merger to date — plus a growing statistical case that some merging black holes are themselves the products of earlier mergers, rather than simple stellar collapse. With new detections now arriving several times a week, gravitational-wave astronomy has moved from rare discovery to routine census-taking of the universe's most violent collisions.

related.title: Gravitational Waves: Ripples in Spacetime
related.hook: When black holes collide, they shake the fabric of spacetime itself, sending out ripples that stretch and squeeze everything they pass — by less than the width of a proton.

related.title: Ten Years of Listening to Black Holes Spin
related.hook: A decade after the first gravitational-wave detection, 100+ events let astronomers read black holes' spins — and spin turns out to reveal how the pairs were born.

related.title: Black Holes
related.hook: A black hole is a place where gravity wins so completely that nothing — not even light — can escape once it crosses the edge called the event horizon.

related.title: Could This Odd LIGO Signal Be the Missing Dark Matter?
related.hook: An unusual gravitational-wave signal has revived a long-shot idea: that primordial black holes born moments after the Big Bang could be the universe's missing dark matter.
